design_detail: Cross-sectional national household survey (the National Comorbidity Survey, NCS): a stratified multistage area probability sample of the noninstitutionalized civilian population aged 15–54 in the 48 coterminous United States, including students in campus group housing; fieldwork 14 September 1990 to 6 February 1992; 8,098 participants, response rate 82.4%. Trained lay interviewers administered the NCS version of the Composite International Diagnostic Interview (CIDI) for DSM-III-R dependence on tobacco, alcohol, eight classes of controlled drugs and inhalants. For each class the paper reports the weighted lifetime prevalence of extramedical use and of dependence, and their ratio: the proportion of people who had ever used the class extramedically who had ever been dependent on it. Tobacco dependence was assessed in a subsample of 4,414 and tobacco use was taken from the 1991 National Household Survey on Drug Abuse. Table 3 gives odds ratios for sociodemographic correlates of dependence. The PDF is a scanned copy with an OCR text layer; every table value cited here was checked against the page image.
can_establish: The weighted lifetime prevalence of extramedical use and of DSM-III-R dependence for each drug class in the US noninstitutionalized population aged 15–54 in 1990–1992, and the proportion of people who had ever used each class who had met dependence criteria at any time up to the interview.
cannot_establish: The probability of becoming dependent after starting use (the ratio is a cross-sectional proportion among everyone who had ever used, including recent starters and people who used a few times, not a cumulative risk); anything specific to methamphetamine (grouped with other non-cocaine stimulants, including prescription stimulants used extramedically); present-day figures (1990–1992 data, DSM-III-R criteria); or causes of the correlates of dependence (cross-sectional).

sample.recruitment: Household probability sample (stratified, multistage area sample released in six replicate subsamples); fieldwork by the University of Michigan Survey Research Center; interviews mostly in the respondent's home (pp. 245–246).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 15–54, noninstitutionalized civilian residents of the 48 coterminous states, including students in campus group housing (p. 245).
sample.demographics: Unweighted sample: 3,847 men and 4,251 women; aged 15–24, 1,768; 25–34, 2,626; 35–44, 2,242; 45–54, 1,462; White 6,084, Black 1,011, Hispanic 733, other 270 (Table 1, p. 250).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview). A supplementary survey of a random subsample of initial non-respondents, with a short-form interview, informed the non-response adjustment (p. 246).
sample.selection_effects: The frame excludes people in institutions (prisons, hospitals), people without a dwelling, people aged 55 or over and, by design, people who had died; the authors cite earlier evidence that including institutional residents changes overall prevalence little, but not for groups with high rates of drug-related incarceration (p. 265). Under-reporting of use or of dependence symptoms is possible; the authors expect incomplete reporting of dependence to lower the proportions (p. 263).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported lifetime extramedical use, asked with questions modelled on the National Household Survey on Drug Abuse and read by the interviewer, with a description of each drug class and a list of qualifying drugs but no pill card; extramedical use covered use without one's own prescription, in greater amounts or more often than prescribed, or for other reasons than a doctor advised (p. 246). The class studied here is psychostimulants other than cocaine, with dextroamphetamine and methamphetamine as the examples given.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequency, recency and age of onset were asked but are not reported in this paper. The dependence questions were asked when participants reported more than a few occasions of use (p. 248).
exposure.polysubstance: Each class is analysed separately; overlap between classes is not reported. An aggregate category of any controlled substance or inhalant is reported (51.0% use, 7.5% dependence, 14.7% dependence among people who had used).

comparison.controls: Not applicable (descriptive); comparisons are between drug classes and between sociodemographic groups.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the prevalence estimates. The odds ratios for correlates are cross-sectional, and the authors caution against reading them causally (p. 259).

outcomes.instruments: CIDI (NCS version) administered by 158 trained lay interviewers and scored by computer algorithm for lifetime DSM-III-R dependence: at least 3 of the 9 Criterion A manifestations plus Criterion B (pp. 246–247). Tobacco: a parallel CIDI section on daily smoking, added midway through fieldwork for a subsample of 4,414 people (55%) (p. 248).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors cite WHO field trials and other studies showing acceptable inter-rater and test–retest reliability and agreement with independent clinical diagnoses (p. 247); there is no validation within this survey, and no informant interviews or bioassays (p. 265).
outcomes.operationalization: Lifetime DSM-III-R dependence by the CIDI algorithm. Dependence among people who had used = the weighted lifetime prevalence of dependence divided by the weighted lifetime prevalence of extramedical use on at least one occasion (p. 248).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable to the 11 prevalence estimates (ten drug classes and the aggregate). The 87 odds ratios of Table 3 are flagged at p < .05 without correction.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Interviewers were not told the study's hypotheses (p. 246); diagnoses were scored by computer.

analysis.effect_sizes: Weighted proportions with standard errors from Taylor-series linearization (Table 2, p. 251). Proportion ever dependent among people who had ever used extramedically: tobacco 31.9% (no SE), alcohol 15.4% (SE 0.7), any controlled substance or inhalant 14.7% (0.7), cannabis 9.1% (0.7), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), psychostimulants other than cocaine 11.2% (1.6), anxiolytics, sedatives and hypnotics 9.2% (1.1), analgesics 7.5% (1.0), psychedelics 4.9% (0.7), heroin 23.1% (5.6), inhalants 3.7% (1.4). Stimulants: lifetime extramedical use 15.3% (0.7) and lifetime dependence 1.7% (0.3) of the population. By age (Table 4, p. 256), stimulant dependence among people who had used: 13.5% (2.9) at 15–24, 13.9% (3.2) at 25–34, 7.7% (1.7) at 35–44 and 6.5% (2.0) at 45–54. By sex (Table 5, p. 259): men 9.7% (1.9), women 13.3% (2.0). Editors' calculation: 95% CI for the stimulant proportion about 8.1% to 14.3% (estimate ± 1.96 SE); the printed ratios match dependence prevalence divided by use prevalence within rounding.
analysis.covariates: Survey weights for selection probability and post-stratification for non-response. Table 3 gives an odds ratio for each characteristic; three multivariable checks are described with their data not shown (pp. 251–253): for race, for unemployment and for education.
analysis.selective_reporting: Frequency and recency of use were collected but are not reported; three multivariable checks (pp. 251–253) and the comparison with the 1991 NHSDA (p. 258) are described without their data. No class-specific figure appears in the abstract.
analysis.power: Not applicable; precision is given by the standard errors (1.6 percentage points for the stimulant proportion).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 1990–1992, about 1 in 9 people aged 15–54 who had ever used non-cocaine stimulants extramedically (11.2%) had ever met DSM-III-R dependence criteria: fewer than for tobacco (31.9%), heroin (23.1%), cocaine (16.7%) or alcohol (15.4%), and more than for cannabis (9.1%). The proportion was lower in people aged 35–54 who had used stimulants (7.7% and 6.5%) than in younger people (13.5% and 13.9%).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract gives about 15% for dependence among people who used drugs other than tobacco and alcohol, the aggregate figure, without class-specific values (p. 244). The discussion concludes that many people who use drugs, perhaps a vast majority, do not seem to become dependent (p. 265), and states that for drugs known for their dependence liability (tobacco, cocaine, heroin) the proportion was 20–40% (p. 263), although Table 2 gives 16.7% for cocaine. The proportions are cross-sectional and include people who had used only once or had started recently, so they describe history at the interview rather than a lifetime risk; the authors discuss survival and recall effects that could move them in either direction (pp. 264–265). Describing the ratio as the transition from use to dependence invites a reading as risk that the design does not measure.

timeline.event: Epidemiologic Catchment Area surveys: close to 20% of people who had used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically more than five times had DSM-III abuse or dependence (Anthony and Trinkoff, 1989, as cited on p. 263; not read).

Epidemiologic Catchment Area lifetime prevalence of dependence on psychostimulants other than cocaine 1.7%, the same as in the NCS, although the ECA used DSM-III criteria and the NCS DSM-III-R (Anthony and Helzer, 1991, as cited on p. 258; not read).
This survey: 11.2% of people who had ever used non-cocaine stimulants extramedically had ever been dependent on them.
NESARC survival analysis of the cumulative probability of dependence after first use for nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine, with no estimate for amphetamine-type stimulants

replication.where_it_stands: The NCS ratio for non-cocaine stimulants is the figure for amphetamine-type stimulants that this project has: the later NESARC analysis (López-Quintero et al., 2011) gives cumulative probabilities for other drugs but none for these stimulants, and no methamphetamine-specific figure from a general-population survey has yet been read. The lifetime prevalence of stimulant dependence matched the earlier ECA surveys (1.7% in both), as reported by the same first author.

Grant Foundation grant 90135190; preparation of the article was supported by the National Institute on Drug Abuse Addiction Research Center (p. 244).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: First author at the Etiology Branch of the NIDA Addiction Research Center and Johns Hopkins University; co-authors at the Institute for Social Research, University of Michigan (p. 244). The article is marked as in the public domain. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A contemporary general-population cohort, or a survey with retrospective age-of-onset data analysed by survival methods, that separates methamphetamine from other stimulants and reports the cumulative probability of DSM-5 or ICD-11 dependence after first use by frequency of use and route, with supplementary samples of the groups that household frames miss (people who are incarcerated or unhoused).

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: A national probability frame of noninstitutionalized civilians aged 15–54, but it excludes people in institutions, people without a dwelling, people aged 55 or over and, by design, people who had died, groups in which stimulant dependence may be more common (p. 265).
Stratified multistage area probability sampling in replicate subsamples, with survey weights.
8,098 participants; the stimulant proportion has a standard error of 1.6 points, the age- and sex-specific ones 1.7 to 3.2.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Table 1 and the methods describe the sample, the fieldwork and the measures.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Response 82.4%, with a non-response survey and post-stratification weights.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: A standardized CIDI with cited reliability, but lay-administered self-report without informants or biological verification; the dependence questions were asked only of people reporting more than a few occasions of use, a threshold described inconsistently (pp. 247–248).

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Identical questions for alcohol, controlled substances and inhalants; tobacco was measured differently (subsample, daily smoking only, use prevalence from another survey), which weakens comparisons with tobacco.
Complex-survey weights, Taylor-series standard errors for proportions and balanced repeated replication for odds ratios; no standard error for the tobacco proportion.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: 82.4%, with a non-response survey and weighting.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A national probability survey with a high response rate, a standardized diagnostic interview applied identically across drug classes and design-based standard errors: as a description of what it measured it is at low risk of bias. The limits that matter are of interpretation and directness: the ratio is a snapshot among everyone who had ever used, not a risk after starting; the stimulant class is not methamphetamine; the frame excludes groups with heavy use; and tobacco was measured differently from the other drugs. It may be cited for the 1990–1992 proportions with these labels.

key_findings.finding: Stratified multistage area probability sample of the noninstitutionalized civilian population aged 15–54 in the 48 coterminous states, fieldwork 14 September 1990 to 6 February 1992; response rate 82.4%, 8,098 participants.
key_findings.locator: Method and Materials, 1st paragraph (p. 245, continuing on p. 246)

key_findings.finding: Drug classes followed NHSDA conventions; the stimulant class is psychostimulants other than cocaine, with dextroamphetamine and methamphetamine as examples, and extramedical use covers use without one's own prescription, in greater amounts or more often than prescribed, or for other reasons than a doctor advised.
key_findings.locator: Method and Materials › Assessment of Alcohol and Other Drug Use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Lifetime DSM-III-R dependence was scored by computer from the lay-administered CIDI (at least 3 of 9 Criterion A manifestations plus Criterion B), with identical questions for alcohol, controlled substances and inhalants; the dependence questions were asked when participants reported at least several occasions of extramedical use, on the assumption that dependence is extremely rare after no more than several uses.
key_findings.locator: Method and Materials › Diagnostic Assessment of Alcohol and Other Drug Dependence, 1st–4th paragraphs (the 4th begins on p. 247 and continues on p. 248)
key_findings.note: The 3rd paragraph (p. 247) says the assessment was given whenever participants reported occasions of extramedical use; the exact threshold is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Tobacco dependence was assessed, for daily smoking only, in a subsample of 4,414 participants (55%); tobacco use came from the 1991 National Household Survey on Drug Abuse, so the tobacco proportion was obtained by division and has no standard error.
key_findings.locator: Method and Materials › Assessment of Tobacco Use and Dependence, 1st–2nd paragraphs; Analysis Procedures, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Proportion ever dependent among people who had ever used extramedically: psychostimulants other than cocaine 11.2% (SE 1.6), with lifetime use 15.3% (0.7) and lifetime dependence 1.7% (0.3) of the population; tobacco 31.9% (no SE), alcohol 15.4% (0.7), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), cannabis 9.1% (0.7), heroin 23.1% (5.6), any controlled substance or inhalant 14.7% (0.7).
key_findings.note: Values checked against the page image (the text layer is OCR). Editors' calculation: 95% CI for the stimulant proportion about 8.1% to 14.3%.

key_findings.finding: The text restates the stimulant figures: 15.3% had used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically and 11.2% of them had developed dependence.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use and the Transition to Drug Dependence, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: By age, the proportion dependent among people who had used stimulants was 13.5% (SE 2.9) at 15–24, 13.9% (3.2) at 25–34, 7.7% (1.7) at 35–44 and 6.5% (2.0) at 45–54.
By sex, the proportion dependent among people who had used stimulants was 9.7% (SE 1.9) in men and 13.3% (2.0) in women; lifetime use was 18.4% and 12.2%.
key_findings.note: The text does not comment on the stimulant sex difference.

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that many people who use drugs, perhaps a vast majority, do not seem to make the transition to dependence, calling this an increasingly well-documented observation; earlier, they state that even for drugs known for their dependence liability (tobacco, cocaine, heroin) 20–40% of people who used had become dependent.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Transition From Drug Use to Drug Dependence, 2nd paragraph (p. 263); Future Directions for Research and Other Implications, 6th (last) paragraph (p. 265)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: cross-sectional design with retrospective self-report, which misses people who have died and those who do not recall or report their drug use; possible incomplete reporting of dependence problems, which would lower the proportions; a frame restricted to noninstitutionalized residents; no informants or bioassays.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Transition From Drug Use to Drug Dependence, 2nd paragraph (p. 263); Future Directions for Research and Other Implications, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (pp. 264–265)

key_findings.finding: The lifetime prevalence of dependence on psychostimulants other than cocaine was 1.7% in both the NCS and the earlier Epidemiologic Catchment Area surveys.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Comparison of Prevalence Estimates, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: The ECA surveys used DSM-III criteria and the NCS DSM-III-R (the paper attributes part of the cocaine difference to this change, p. 258), so the match of 1.7% is across diagnostic systems.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion states that for drugs known for their dependence liability (tobacco, cocaine, heroin) the proportion of people who used who became dependent was 20–40%, but Table 2 gives 16.7% for cocaine.
reporting_issues.consequence: The range overstates the cocaine figure; only cocaine use at ages 15–24 (24.5%, Table 4) falls inside it.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion describes a sharp drop in the prevalence of heroin dependence from 2.7% at 35–44 to 0.7% at 45–54, but in Table 4 these are the prevalences of heroin use; dependence was 0.8% and 0.1%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use mislabelled as dependence; the argument about premature mortality is unaffected in direction.

reporting_issues.issue: The analgesic figures (9.7% use, 7.5% dependence among people who used) are cited to Table 3, columns 4 and 6, but they are in Table 2; Table 3 holds odds ratios.

The discussion states that sex differences in dependence among people who had used were found only for alcohol and cannabis, but the results (pp. 255, 257) and Table 5 (p. 259) report a difference for anxiolytics, sedatives and hypnotics (6.6% in men, 12.3% in women); the stimulant difference (9.7% vs 13.3%) is not discussed anywhere.
reporting_issues.consequence: Internal inconsistency; for stimulants the sex-specific figures should be read from Table 5.

reporting_issues.issue: The threshold for administering the dependence questions is described as any reported occasions of extramedical use (p. 247) and as at least several occasions (p. 248), without an exact number.
reporting_issues.consequence: People with only a few occasions of use are counted as not dependent without assessment; this barely affects the proportions if dependence after so few uses is as rare as assumed, but the rule cannot be reproduced.

reporting_issues.issue: The tobacco footnote of Tables 4 and 5 (printed under Table 4 on p. 257 and under Table 5 on p. 259) attributes tobacco use to the 1991 National Household Survey on Drug Use and then gives n = 4,414, which could be read as the size of that survey's sample; in the text 4,414 is the NCS tobacco-dependence subsample (p. 248), and the survey is named the National Household Survey on Drug Abuse. The footnote also sends readers to the section on alcohol and other drug use for the tobacco method, which is described under the tobacco assessment heading (p. 248). Tables 2 and 4 also order their columns differently (dependence before use in Table 2, use before dependence in Table 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; a risk of misreading the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: Three odds ratios in the Results text differ from Table 3 (p. 252): for tobacco dependence among African Americans the text gives 0.59 (p. 251) and the table 0.45 (0.59 is the table's Hispanic value); for people living with a spouse the text gives 0.87 (p. 253) and the table 1.05 (0.87 is the value for living with others); and for incomes of $20,000 to $34,000 the text gives 1.43, printed with the interval of the table's 1.44 (p. 253).
reporting_issues.consequence: One figure in each pair is in error and the source does not say which; none concerns stimulants, so the stimulant figures are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 prints an estimate of dependence among people who had used heroin, at ages 45 and over (10.7%, SE 7.7), although the text says there were too few people aged 45–54 who had used heroin (13, one of them with a history of dependence) to produce such an estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed cell comes from 13 people, one with a history of dependence, and is unreliable; it does not affect the stimulant rows.
